watchouts: A one-off disclosure buried in onboarding does not cover a voice that meets a fresh person on every call — each natural person concerned must be informed at first contact.
The duty belongs to the provider: the disclosure has to be built into the system, not left to the user to volunteer.

scenarios.title: A utility's chatbot that poses as staff
scenarios.summary: An energy supplier replaces its first-line email support with a generative chatbot that answers billing questions and opens disputes in conversational prose.

roles.who: The supplier, if it builds the assistant in-house; otherwise the software vendor that supplies it.
The energy supplier operating it on its website and app.
Customers seeking help with bills or complaints.

analysis.title: Direct interaction triggers Article 50(1)
analysis.detail: A customer typing into a chatbot is interacting directly with an AI system, so the system must be designed to tell them so unless that is obvious from the circumstances.

analysis.title: Not high-risk
analysis.detail: Customer service is not an Annex III use and the chatbot is not a safety component of an Annex I product, so the Chapter III regime does not apply.

analysis.title: Synthetic text carries a separate marking duty
analysis.detail: Because the system generates text content, the provider must also ensure its outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated — a provider-side duty distinct from the interaction disclosure.

analysis.title: AI literacy still applies
analysis.detail: Providers and deployers must ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy among the staff and other persons dealing with the system on their behalf.

watchouts: "Limited risk" is light, not nil: both the disclosure duty and the marking duty are enforceable.
The marking duty sits with the provider of the system that generates the text, which is not necessarily the deployer operating the chatbot.

scenarios.title: A wellbeing app that reads your mood
scenarios.summary: A consumer app infers a user's emotional state from voice notes and usage signals to recommend mindfulness exercises. The identical feature aimed at employees would be banned outright.

roles.who: The app developer placing the emotion-inference system on the market.
The same company, operating the system on the people it infers from.
The users whose emotional state is inferred.

analysis.title: Emotion recognition, so Article 50(3) bites
analysis.detail: Deployers of an emotion recognition system must inform the natural persons exposed to it that it is operating, and must process the personal data in line with the applicable data-protection rules.

analysis.title: It is the deployer's duty
analysis.detail: Article 50(3) is addressed to the deployer — the party operating the system on the people concerned — so disclosure is an operational obligation, not only a design one.

analysis.title: At work the same feature would be prohibited
analysis.detail: Inferring emotions of a natural person in the workplace or in education institutions is banned outright, except where the system is used for medical or safety reasons. A consumer wellbeing app escapes that ban only because it is used neither at work nor in school.

analysis.title: Not high-risk by itself
analysis.detail: Consumer emotion inference is not listed in Annex III and is not an Annex I safety component, so the Chapter III regime does not apply — only the transparency duty does.

watchouts: The dividing line is the area of use, not the technology: the same model is a transparency case at home and a prohibited practice in the workplace or a classroom.
Disclosure must reach everyone exposed, at the latest at first exposure, and the data-protection rules apply in parallel.

scenarios.title: A deepfake star endorsing a product
scenarios.summary: A marketing agency generates a video in which a famous actor's face and voice appear to endorse a product he has never seen, and publishes it as an ordinary advertisement.

roles.who: The developer of the video-generation model used to make the clip.
The marketing agency producing and publishing the advertisement.
The audience, and the celebrity whose likeness is reproduced.

analysis.title: It is a deepfake, so the deployer must disclose
analysis.detail: Deployers of a system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

analysis.title: The provider must mark the output machine-readable
analysis.detail: Independently of the agency's disclosure, the provider of the generating system must ensure its outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

analysis.title: The artistic carve-out is thin here
analysis.detail: Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional work, the duty narrows to disclosing the manipulated content without spoiling the work. A straight endorsement advertisement is not such a work.

analysis.title: Advertising is not an Annex III use
analysis.detail: The system is not an Annex I safety component and does not fall within the Annex III list, so the obligation is transparency only.

watchouts: Publishing a real person's likeness without consent also engages personality and data-protection law, which the Act does not displace.
Labeling the video as AI-generated does not make an unauthorised use of a real person's face and voice lawful.

scenarios.title: AI-written summaries of the news
scenarios.summary: A news aggregator automatically generates summaries of political and economic stories to inform the public, with no editor reviewing the text before it is published.

roles.who: The developer of the text-generation system.
The aggregator publishing the summaries.
The reading public.

analysis.title: Public-interest text must be labelled
analysis.detail: Deployers that generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated.

analysis.title: The editorial-control exception does not apply
analysis.detail: The duty falls away only where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication. An unreviewed publishing pipeline cannot rely on it.

analysis.title: The generating provider marks the output
analysis.detail: Separately, the provider of the text-generating system must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated.

analysis.title: Not high-risk
analysis.detail: Aggregating and summarising news is not an Annex III use and is not an Annex I safety component, so only the transparency duty applies.

watchouts: The exception turns on genuine editorial responsibility, not a nominal editor drawn on the workflow diagram.
The disclosure must be clear and distinguishable and reach the reader at the latest at first exposure to the text.

scenarios.title: A downloadable open-weights model
scenarios.summary: A research lab releases a general-purpose language model under a free and open-source licence, with the weights, architecture and usage information posted publicly for anyone to download.

roles.who: The lab that develops and releases the model.
Developers who download the model and build AI systems on it.
Users of the resulting systems.

analysis.title: A general-purpose model, so Article 53 applies
analysis.detail: A model that displays significant generality and can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks is a general-purpose AI model, and its provider carries the Article 53 obligations.

analysis.title: Open weights lighten two of the four duties
analysis.detail: The technical-documentation duty in Article 53(1)(a), set out in Annex XI, and the downstream-information duty in Article 53(1)(b), set out in Annex XII, do not apply to a model released under a free and open-source licence whose weights, architecture and usage information are made publicly available.

analysis.title: Two duties survive even for open weights
analysis.detail: The copyright-compliance policy and the public summary of training content are not disapplied, so an open-weights release still needs both.

analysis.title: The exemption is conditional
analysis.detail: It depends on a licence that genuinely allows access, use, modification and distribution, and it stops applying altogether once the model meets the systemic-risk threshold.

watchouts: A gated or restricted download is not an open-source release, so the exemption may not be available.
A downstream developer that fine-tunes the model and releases its own version may become a provider with its own Article 53 duties.

scenarios.title: The same model above the compute threshold
scenarios.summary: The lab's next release uses cumulative training compute above 10^25 floating-point operations, so the general-purpose model is presumed to carry systemic risk and the open-source carve-out falls away.

roles.who: The lab, now subject to the systemic-risk regime.
The Union body it must report serious incidents to.
Those integrating the model into their own systems.

analysis.title: The compute threshold triggers the regime
analysis.detail: A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have systemic risk where the cumulative compute used for training exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, and the provider must notify the Commission without delay.

analysis.title: Everything in Article 53 still applies
analysis.detail: The systemic-risk duties are additional to, not instead of, the baseline documentation, downstream-information, copyright and training-summary duties.

analysis.title: Evaluation, mitigation, incident reporting, cybersecurity
analysis.detail: The provider must perform model evaluation including documented adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level, track and report serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection.

analysis.title: The open-source exemption no longer helps
analysis.detail: The carve-out from the Article 53(1)(a) and (b) duties expressly does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.

watchouts: The compute figure is a rebuttable presumption — the provider may argue it away before the Commission, but the notification duty stands.
A provider established outside the Union must appoint an authorised representative in the Union before placing the model on the market.

scenarios.title: Fine-tuning someone else's model and selling it
scenarios.summary: A startup takes an open-weights general-purpose model, fine-tunes it on domain data, brands it and puts the resulting model on the market as its own product.

roles.who: The startup, once it places the fine-tuned model on the market under its own name.
The lab that released the original model.
Developers who build products on the fine-tuned model.

analysis.title: Releasing your own model makes you the provider
analysis.detail: A party that develops a general-purpose AI model and places it on the market is its provider. Putting a modified model on the market under your own name is what draws the Article 53 duties to you.

analysis.title: A copyright policy is mandatory
analysis.detail: The provider must put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, including identifying and honouring a reservation of rights for text and data mining.

analysis.title: A public training-content summary is mandatory
analysis.detail: The provider must draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, following the template provided by the AI Office — covering the fine-tuning data as well as the base model's.

analysis.title: You lean on the upstream documentation
analysis.detail: The upstream provider must supply the documentation that lets downstream providers understand the model's capabilities and limitations, but the downstream provider still owns the duties it triggers by releasing its own model.

watchouts: The upstream provider's own compliance does not transfer: each provider answers for the model it places on the market.
If the fine-tuned model is released only inside an AI system, the analysis changes — it is placing the model itself on the market that engages Article 53.

scenarios.title: An email spam filter
scenarios.summary: A mail provider runs a machine-learning classifier that sorts incoming messages into inbox and spam.

roles.who: The mail provider, or the vendor of the filtering engine.
The mailbox owner whose mail is filtered.

analysis.title: No Annex III use
analysis.detail: Sorting email for spam is not one of the Annex III use cases, and the classifier is not a safety component of an Annex I product, so it is not high-risk.

analysis.title: No Article 50 trigger
analysis.detail: A spam filter does not interact directly with people in the transparency sense, does not generate synthetic media, and does not perform emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, so no disclosure duty arises.

analysis.title: Voluntary codes of conduct
analysis.detail: Providers of systems outside the mandatory regimes are encouraged to apply codes of conduct voluntarily, drawing on the Chapter III requirements and on Union ethical guidelines for trustworthy AI.

analysis.title: AI literacy still applies
analysis.detail: Even with no risk-tier obligations, providers and deployers must take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy among the people dealing with the system.

watchouts: "Out of scope" means outside the Act's mandatory regimes — data-protection and consumer law still apply.
If the same classifier were repurposed to profile or rank people rather than messages, the analysis would change.

scenarios.title: Demand forecasting for a corner shop
scenarios.summary: A small grocery uses an off-the-shelf tool that predicts which products will sell, to decide what to reorder.

roles.who: The vendor of the forecasting tool.
The shop owner.

analysis.title: Not an Annex III use
analysis.detail: Forecasting stock demand is not a listed Annex III purpose and the tool is not a safety component of an Annex I product, so the Chapter III regime does not apply.

analysis.title: No Article 50 trigger
analysis.detail: The tool does not converse with people, generate synthetic content, or infer emotions or biometric traits, so none of the transparency duties apply.

analysis.title: Voluntary codes remain open
analysis.detail: The provider may voluntarily adopt a code of conduct, for example on energy efficiency or trustworthy-AI practices.

analysis.title: AI literacy is universal
analysis.detail: The literacy duty in Article 4 applies to every provider and deployer, whatever the tier.

watchouts: A tool that forecasts aggregate demand is minimal-risk; one that scores or profiles individual people could move up the ladder.
Small scale is not itself the test — the intended purpose and the context of use decide the tier.

scenarios.title: Predicting crop yield from satellite imagery
scenarios.summary: An agritech platform analyses satellite imagery and weather data to forecast harvest yields for farms and agricultural insurers.

roles.who: The agritech company building the model.
Farms and agricultural insurers using the forecasts.
Farmers relying on the forecast for planning.

analysis.title: No Annex III listing fits
analysis.detail: Crop-yield forecasting is not among the Annex III use cases, and the system is not a safety component of an Annex I product, so it is not high-risk. It does not evaluate people at all.

analysis.title: No Article 50 trigger
analysis.detail: The system analyses land and weather, not people: it does not interact with users conversationally, generate synthetic media, or infer emotions, so transparency duties do not bite.

analysis.title: Voluntary codes of conduct
analysis.detail: Even outside the mandatory regimes, the provider is encouraged to follow a code of conduct, which can cover environmental sustainability and trustworthy-AI practices.

analysis.title: AI literacy still applies
analysis.detail: Everyone who operates the system on the provider's or deployer's behalf must be supported with a sufficient level of AI literacy.

watchouts: Remote-sensing and geospatial systems have no Annex III entry; a system that instead scored farmers as individuals would need a fresh classification.
The absence of AI Act obligations does not displace data-protection law, where the data relates to identifiable people.

governance_structure.title: Who governs the Act
governance_structure.note: Solid lines are institutional; the advisory forum's role is advisory to both the Commission and the Board.

children.name: European Commission
children.note: Develops Union expertise and capability in AI.

children.name: AI Office
children.note: Oversees general-purpose AI models, coordinates and enforces at Union level; attends the Board without voting.

children.name: Scientific panel of independent experts
children.note: Supports enforcement; independent of AI providers; Member States may call on it and pay fees.

children.name: European Artificial Intelligence Board
children.note: One representative per Member State; the EDPS participates as observer; the AI Office attends without voting.

children.name: Advises and assists the Commission and Member States
children.note: Coordinates national authorities, shares expertise, advises on GPAI enforcement and on sandboxes and real-world testing.

children.name: Advisory forum
children.note: Balanced stakeholders: industry, start-ups, SMEs, civil society and academia. Advises the Board and the Commission.

children.name: National competent authorities
children.note: Each Member State designates at least one notifying authority and one market surveillance authority, acting independently and impartially.

children.name: Notifying authorities
children.note: Assess, designate and monitor notified bodies.

children.name: Market surveillance authorities
children.note: Enforce the Act in the market, receive serious-incident reports and fundamental rights impact assessments.

children.name: Single points of contact
children.note: Each Member State designates a single point of contact for the public and for stakeholders.
